title: Matchscore-based kernel routing and fragment reshuffle for prefill coalescence
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem statement:
Paged attention workloads show pathological latency and token-cost increases when tenants produce many partially overlapping prefill sequences. Current page allocation and eviction operate on recency/occupancy heuristics which cause: (1) repeated reassembly of small fragments across different kernels, (2) incompatible kernel selection due to fragment alignment, and (3) decode waves that cannot coalesce prefill work, increasing kernel launch overhead and memory thrashing.

Goal:
Design and implement a matchscore-driven kernel routing and fragment reshuffle subsystem to increase prefill coalescence, reduce KV fragmentation, and improve decode latency and per-token cost for multi-tenant/prefix-heavy workloads. Target improvements: 15-25% tail latency reduction at p95/p99 and 10-20% reduction in token GPU time for representative PLG workloads.

Proposed approach (high level):
1) Matchscore index: compute a lightweight fingerprint per KV fragment (shape, model-variant, quantization-profile, sequence-anchor) and maintain a per-shard matchscore index that ranks compatibility between incoming prefill requests and resident fragments. The index is bounded (LRU+age buckets) and optimized for single-shot lookups in the hotpath.

2) Collision-aware fragment reshuffle: when allocation or eviction would create many small, incompatible fragments, attempt a bounded-cost reshuffle that coalesces adjacent fragments with compatible matchscore ranges. Reshuffle operates opportunistically during low-GPU-util windows or as a background microtransaction that yields on budget.

3) Kernel matchscore routing: use the matchscore to prefer kernel variants and co-placement strategies that will maximize shared decode kernels across concurrently arriving prefill requests (e.g., prefer variant A for fragments where matchscore>t1 so multiple requests can be handled by the same kernel instance).

4) Prefill overlap detector + batching hints: detect when incoming prefill requests share token prefixes or KV affinity and issue batching hints to the runtime (soft grouping) that enable denser decode-wave packing without sacrificing tail latency SLOs.

Design notes and tradeoffs:
- Index maintenance costs vs. hit-rate: the matchscore index must be cheap; we use 32-bit fingerprints and a 4-level age ladder. There is an upfront CPU cost for fingerprinting on allocation/eviction but the expected win is in reduced GPU work.
- Reshuffle safety: reshuffle must preserve decoder correctness and memory safety. Plan to use copy-on-write for live fragments and only reshuffle cold-to-warm transitions or fragments pinned under a lease.
- Kernel selection policy complexity: adding matchscore into kernel selection increases combinatorial options. We will start with a thresholded preference model (prefer same-kernel if compatibility score >= X) rather than full cost-based solver.

Implementation plan (phases):
Phase 1 (prototype, 2 sprints):
- Implement 32-bit fragment fingerprinting and per-shard matchscore index (read-optimized).
- Instrument allocation path to compute fingerprint and publish into index.
- Add telemetry: matchscore hit/miss, fingerprint churn, fragment-size histogram.

Phase 2 (safety + microbench, 1 sprint):
- Add unit tests for fingerprint collisions and kernel-routing fallbacks.
- Build small microbench harness that replays production prefix traces (sanitized) to validate matchscore hit-rate and CPU overhead.

Phase 3 (reshuffle + routing, 2 sprints):
- Implement bounded fragment reshuffle with configurable budget per shard.
- Integrate routing preference into kernel selector; add configuration knobs for threshold and budget.
- End-to-end integration tests with prefill overlap detector and batching hints.

Phase 4 (canary rollout, 1 sprint):
- Canary in dedicated pool with 10% traffic; compare p95/p99 latency, token GPU-time, and eviction rates vs baseline.
- Gradual ramp following data validation and no regressions in correctness.

Metrics and success criteria:
- p95/p99 decode latency reduced by >=15% in canary relative to baseline for prefix-heavy workloads.
- Token GPU-time reduced by >=10% on test traces.
- Fragment count and average fragment size improve: target 20% fewer fragments and 1.5x average fragment size in steady state.
- CPU overhead for matchscore maintenance < 5% of host CPU at 95th percentile for per-shard maintenance.

Risks and mitigations:
- Fingerprint collisions leading to incorrect co-placement: mitigate by using conservative routing fallbacks and a short verification handshake on kernel match.
- Reshuffle causing spikes in GPU memory pressure: limit reshuffle to windows where free budget > threshold and expose config to disable reshuffle per-tenant.
- Unexpected interaction with KV-prefetch heuristics: coordinate with prefetch team (ENG-98114) and add compatibility tests.

Artifacts and links:
- Design doc (internal): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Matchscore+Routing+Design
- Trace replay harness PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4126
- Prototype microbench results snapshot: https://dashboards.redwood.ai/d/prefill/frag-reshuffle-2026-03-01

Next steps (short term):
- Land fingerprinting and telemetry (week 1).
- Run replay harness across 3 representative tenants and collect hit-rate and CPU numbers (week 2).
- Decide threshold X and initial reshuffle budget based on microbench results (week 3).
